extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal definitions for working with ordered pairs, Cartesian products, truth sets, and relations, together with proof strategies (element chasing, proof by cases, contradiction, handling existentials) used in introductory set theory / discrete math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cartesian product
rubrics_metrics.description: Ax B = {(a,b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If A = {red, green} and B = {2,3,5} then A x B = {(red,2),(red,3),(red,5),(green,2),(green,3),(green,5)}. If P = set of people then P x N = {(p,n)| p is a person and n is a natural number}. The set A x B consists of ordered pairs whose first coordinate comes from A and second from B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equality: mutual inclusion or elementwise biconditional
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets are equal you can either prove ∀p[p ∈ X ↔ p ∈ Y] (stringing together equivalences) or prove both inclusions X ⊆ Y and Y ⊆ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates taking the second approach: prove A x (B ∩ C) ⊆ (A x B) ∩ (A x C) and the reverse inclusion. Choose the approach that makes the proof straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce an arbitrary element and use existential instantiation for inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving an inclusion (X ⊆ Y), let p be an arbitrary element of X and then show p ∈ Y. If p turns out to be an ordered pair, introduce its coordinates by existential instantiation (write p = (x,y) for some x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In proving A x (B ∩ C) ⊆ (A x B) ∩ (A x C), let p be arbitrary in A x (B ∩ C); since p is an ordered pair, write p = (x,y) with x ∈ A and y ∈ B ∩ C and proceed by unpacking definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress explicit ordered-pair introduction when obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is clear an object will be an ordered pair, mathematicians often omit the formal step 'p is an ordered pair' and simply write it as (x,y) from the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book follows this convention: when it is evident the arbitrary element must be an ordered pair, call it (x,y) immediately to streamline the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by cases for unions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an arbitrary element belongs to a union (X ∪ Y), handle the statement 'p ∈ X ∪ Y' by breaking into cases: either p ∈ X or p ∈ Y, and prove the goal in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To show (A x B) ∪ (C x D) ⊆ (A ∪ C) x (B ∪ D), take (x,y) in the left-hand union and consider Case 1: (x,y) ∈ A x B, Case 2: (x,y) ∈ C x D; in each case show (x,y) ∈ (A ∪ C) x (B ∪ D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradiction for equalities with the empty set
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a set equals the empty set, assume it has an element and derive a contradiction (i.e., proof by contradiction is natural because equality to ∅ is a negative statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To prove A x ∅ = ∅ assume A x ∅ has an element (x,y); but ∅ has no elements, contradiction. The commentary notes these are negative statements and contradiction is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for empty sets when reasoning from Cartesian-product equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning that A x B = B x A implies A = B, one must consider the possibility that A or B might be empty; informal coordinate-argument can fail if a factor is ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The incorrect informal proof fails if B = ∅ because you cannot pick a y ∈ B. The correct proof handles cases A = ∅ or B = ∅ separately (or assumes nonemptiness to choose elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving biconditionals (iff) by proving two directions
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'iff' statement should be proven by establishing each implication separately: prove (→) and then (←).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For A x B = B x A iff (A = ∅ or B = ∅ or A = B) the text proves the (→) direction under the assumption A ≠ ∅ and B ≠ ∅ to deduce A = B, and then handles the other cases for (←) by case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer working with positive statements; negate negatives via De Morgan
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative statements like 'A = ∅' are often awkward in proofs; it can be clearer to negate them (A ≠ ∅) which are existential and allow introduction of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary: when faced with a disjunction whose negation produces negative statements, use De Morgan's laws to reframe into positive (existential) assumptions so you can choose witnesses (elements) to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of truth set for two-variable statements
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(x,y) is a statement where x ranges over A and y over B, the truth set of P(x,y) is {(a,b) ∈ A x B | P(a,b)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: truth set of 'x has y children' is {(p,n) ∈ P x N | p has n children}; the graph of an equation y = 2x − 3 is the truth set {(x,y) ∈ R x R | y = 2x − 3}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connectives on statements correspond to set operations on truth sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If T is truth set of P(x,y) and S is truth set of Q(x,y), then truth set of P ∧ Q is T ∩ S, truth set of P ∨ Q is T ∪ S; if P true for all x,y then truth set = A x B; if P false for all then truth set = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these correspondences to translate logical reasoning about formulas into set operations on relations/truth sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of relation from A to B
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R from A to B is any R ⊆ A x B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although motivated by truth sets, a relation need not be described syntactically as a statement; any subset of A x B qualifies. Examples include L = {(s,r) ∈ S x R | student s lives in room r}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of domain and range
rubrics_metrics.description: Dom(R) = {a ∈ A | ∃b ∈ B ((a,b) ∈ R)}; Ran(R) = {b ∈ B | ∃a ∈ A ((a,b) ∈ R)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: domain = set of first-coordinates that occur in R (e.g., students who live in some dorm room); range = set of second-coordinates that occur (e.g., occupied rooms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inverse relation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inverse contains same ordered pairs with coordinates reversed. Example: inverse of greater-than relation is less-than relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and domain-requirement for composition of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If R ⊆ A x B and S ⊆ B x C, then S ◦ R = {(a,c) ∈ A x C | ∃b ∈ B ((a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S)}; composition is only defined if the middle sets match (second coordinates of R equal first of S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation: if (s,c) ∈ S ◦ R then there exists b with (s,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S. Beware the notation order: (s,p) ∈ T ◦ E when E maps students to courses and T maps courses to professors (so you can only compose T after E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential statements suggest introducing new variables when proving compositions/associativity
rubrics_metrics.description: When (a,d) ∈ T ◦ (S ◦ R), this is an existential statement '∃c ∈ C ((a,c) ∈ S ◦ R and (c,d) ∈ T)', which suggests introducing a witness c; similarly (a,c) ∈ S ◦ R suggests introducing a witness b. Chain these existentials in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof of associativity T ◦ (S ◦ R) = (T ◦ S) ◦ R uses introducing c then b to build the required witness for the other side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition is associative but not commutative
rubrics_metrics.description: For relations R: A→B, S: B→C, T: C→D, we have T ◦ (S ◦ R) = (T ◦ S) ◦ R (associative), but in general S ◦ R ≠ R ◦ S (not commutative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text proves associativity by chaining existential witnesses; examples earlier show composition results differ when order is swapped, so do not assume commutativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of inverse and domain/range
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs proceed by element-chasing or equivalence chaining: (a,b) ∈ (R^{-1})^{-1} iff (b,a) ∈ R^{-1} iff (a,b) ∈ R, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation xRy to mean (x,y) ∈ R
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of writing (x,y) ∈ R, one often writes x R y to express the relation between x and y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors common mathematical relational notation like x = y, x < y, x ∈ y and is useful when reasoning symbolically about relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictures (vertices and edges) to reason about relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent A and B as ovals with elements as vertices and draw arrows for ordered pairs; edges pointing away from A-vertices identify domain elements, edges pointing to B-vertices identify range elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictures help visualize composition (paths of length two correspond to elements of S ◦ R), domain/range, inverse (reverse arrows). Example figures illustrate students→courses→professors and how T ◦ E corresponds to two-step paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an author claims 'similar' or leaves part as an exercise, verify the omitted details
rubrics_metrics.description: If part of a proof is labeled 'similar' or left to the reader, you should work through the details (in your head or on paper) to ensure the analogous argument really works in that context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly warns that saying 'the proof is similar' doesn't itself prove anything — you must check the omitted half (e.g., second half of Ax∅ = ∅ or OxA = ∅).
